proof:
# Convex subbodies with integer mixed centroids need not retain three quarters

Fix `0<epsilon<1`. In `R x R`, let C be the convex hull of the centered
interval fibers at integer indices `0,1,2` with lengths

    (1,1,epsilon).

The piecewise affine width function is concave, so these are exactly the
integer fibers of C. The body is full dimensional, all three fibers have
positive length, its mixed mass is `M=2+epsilon`, and every fiber has mass
strictly less than `M/2`.

Let D be ANY measurable subset of C with positive mixed mass whose true
mixed centroid has integer base coordinate. Write its retained fiber masses
as `(a,b,c)`, so `0<=a,b<=1`, `0<=c<=epsilon`. Its integer centroid is one
of `0,1,2` because its base support lies in that interval. If it is zero,
then `b+2c=0`, so its mass is at most one. If it is two, the analogous
nonnegative moment identity forces `a=b=0`, and its mass is at most epsilon.
If it is one, the exact moment identity is `c=a`; hence

    mass(D)=2a+b <=1+2epsilon.                          (1)

This proof does not require D to be convex, so it applies in particular to
every convex subbody of C.

The upper bound is attained by an actual full-dimensional convex subbody:
take centered interval lengths `(epsilon,1,epsilon)` at those same indices
and their convex hull. Each generating interval lies in C, the concave width
sequence gives exactly these fibers, and its mixed centroid has base one.
Thus the maximum retained mass with integer mixed centroid is EXACTLY

    1+2epsilon,

and the best retention ratio is `(1+2epsilon)/(2+epsilon)`. It tends to one
half as epsilon decreases to zero and is below three quarters whenever
`epsilon<2/5`. At the rational choice `epsilon=1/10`, the ratio is exactly
`4/7`.

For comparison, the two-fiber product `[0,1] x [0,1]` has the simpler exact
one-half retention obstruction: an integer centroid requires all positive
mass to lie on just one of its two bases. The three-fiber construction above
shows that excluding two-fiber supports and excluding heavy fibers does not
repair a universal three-quarter retention proposal.

Consequently, applying the conditional one-third centroid theorem solely to
a uniformly guaranteed three-quarter-mass convex truncation cannot be a
general point-selection argument. This does not refute the existence of a
deep point in C's mixed set, or any scheme that also uses the original mass
outside the selected subbody.
